raw_response:
I will keep the main frame the same as what has worked for me here: wheat-maize on the biggest block, then a few vegetable and cash crops to bring in money at different times. I have 50 mu, so I do not want too many tiny scattered plots. This year I will put 25 mu into wheat-maize rotation, 5 mu cabbage, 4 mu chili, 4 mu garlic, 4 mu onion, and 8 mu stevia. That way I keep grain for steady output, but I still have enough higher-value crops. I have middle school education and 15 years in the field, so I do not farm only by habit, but I still start from last year and from what I see nearby. Around Quzhou, if wheat and maize are short on fertilizer, yield loss hurts more than spending a bit extra, so on the grain land I will not cut too hard. I have well irrigation, so I will use water to hold yield when the season turns dry.

For wheat, I will use improved seed and keep the stand even. I will put more nitrogen on the wheat-maize land than on stevia, but I will still keep phosphorus and potassium in, because if I push only urea the crop looks green first and then falls off later. For maize after wheat, I will go fast with no-tillage seeding on the same 25 mu so I do not lose moisture and time. For cabbage, chili, garlic, and onion, I will feed heavier on potassium than I do on wheat, because these crops need quality and size, not just a green top. Chili is the one I will watch most closely for insects and disease, so it gets the most spray rounds. Garlic and onion I will keep steady with water and not let them stall. Stevia I will manage more carefully on cost: enough fertilizer and clean field management, but I will not spend like it is cabbage. My basic way is simple: keep the grain land safe, use the well, feed the vegetable crops properly, and avoid making big risky changes in one year.
